_comment: Hardware manifest for the /hardware demonstrator. Single source of truth: the 3D mount positions, sensor coverage volumes, wiring topology, BOM and rover mapping all read from this file. Truck frame is x forward, y left, z up, origin at ground level under the centre of the machine.

components.label: 77 GHz long-range radar
components.role: Detects and tracks moving mass directly ahead, with range and radial velocity measured rather than inferred.
components.fog: Wavelength 3.9 mm against a 10 micrometre droplet, roughly 390 times larger, so Mie scattering is negligible and range is unaffected by fog.
components.rover: HB100 or RCWL-0516 Doppler module. Same physics, no angular resolution.

components.label: Corner radar, left rear
components.role: Covers the reversing and quartering geometry: the tip edge, and the light vehicle behind you.
components.fog: Immune. Reversing at a tip edge is where fog kills people, and it is exactly where the operator has no view.

components.label: Corner radar, right rear
components.role: Mirror of the left corner unit. Together they close the 360 degree near field around the machine.

components.label: LWIR thermal camera
components.role: Classifies what the radar can only call something: a person, a running engine, a hot brake.
components.fog: Degraded but usable. The band is comparable to droplet size, so it loses range, yet keeps warm bodies visible far longer than the eye does.
components.rover: AMG8833 8x8 thermal array. Same band, 64 pixels.

components.label: Visible camera
components.role: Not used for driving. It measures visibility, records evidence for incident replay, and reads signage.
components.fog: Fails as a driving sensor, and that is the point of the whole design. We use it to MEASURE the fog, not to see through it.

components.label: RTK-GNSS antenna
components.part: u-blox ZED-F9P with survey antenna, NTRIP over site LTE
components.role: Two to three centimetres of absolute position. This is what lets the twin know where the road is without seeing it.
components.fog: Completely unaffected. A 19 to 24 cm wavelength passes through cloud as if it were not there.
components.rover: DWM1000 UWB trilateration, because GNSS is useless inside a hall

components.label: IMU and wheel odometry tap
components.part: ADIS16470 or Bosch BMI088, plus J1939 CAN interface
components.role: Bridges GNSS outages at 200 Hz: under the highwall, in the workshop, beside the shovel.
components.fog: Unaffected. Dead reckoning does not care about weather, only about elapsed time.

components.label: UWB tag
components.role: Sub-30 cm ranging where it matters most: the tip edge, the loading bay, the workshop gate. It also ranges to personnel tags.
components.rover: Identical part. This one is production hardware already.

components.label: Edge compute node
components.part: Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB in an IP67 vibration-isolated enclosure
components.role: Sensor fusion, tracking, threat scoring, HUD rendering and the offline twin cache. Every safety-critical decision closes here.
components.fog: This is where the system stops needing to see. It holds the surveyed corridor, so a network drop costs foresight, never braking.
components.rover: Raspberry Pi 4 or ESP32. Same ROS 2 topics, less throughput.

components.label: LTE and C-V2X modem
components.part: Quectel AG55xQ, private LTE plus PC5 sidelink
components.role: Uplinks pose and detections to the nearest roadside unit at 5 Hz, and downlinks neighbours, tokens and speed advisories.
components.fog: Unaffected. Terrain blocks it, not weather, which is why we route through infrastructure rather than peer to peer.
components.rover: ESP32 Wi-Fi, or LoRa for the comms-loss demo

components.label: LoRa safety heartbeat
components.role: Twenty bytes of pose plus an emergency flag, once a second. The link that survives when broadband does not.
components.fog: Unaffected, and non line of sight over 5 to 15 km in this terrain.

components.label: Synthetic-vision display
components.role: Draws the road ahead from surveyed geometry. Readable in under 0.4 seconds, gloved, in a vibrating cab.
components.fog: This is the operator eye when the windscreen has nothing to offer.
components.rover: Any tablet pointed at the same kiosk URL

components.label: Seat haptic transducer
components.part: Tactile transducer pad, armrest and seat base
components.role: A directional warning the operator cannot tune out. Left buzz for a left-side threat.
components.fog: Cab noise runs 85 to 95 dB and operators wear ear protection, so audio alone is unreliable. Haptics are not decoration here.
components.rover: Vibration motor on the demo tablet

components.label: Isolated 24 V power unit
components.part: DC-DC 24 V to 12 V and 5 V, fused and transient protected
components.role: Takes the machine 24 V bus, isolates it, and holds the kit up through cranking dips and load-dump transients.
components.fog: Nothing to do with fog, and everything to do with the kit still being alive after one monsoon.

components.label: Harness, mounts and enclosures
components.part: IP67 glands, automotive connectors, vibration-isolated brackets
components.role: The unglamorous half of a retrofit, and the half that decides whether it survives to the second monsoon.
components.rover: Zip ties and heat shrink, honestly

links.label: UART, RTCM in and NMEA out
SPI at 200 Hz plus J1939 CAN

infrastructure.label: Roadside unit
infrastructure.role: Private LTE cell, C-V2X relay and edge cache on an existing lighting mast. Height and mains power are exactly why we route through these rather than peer to peer.

infrastructure.label: Micro-met station
infrastructure.role: Forward-scatter visibility sensor with temperature, dew point and wind. Calibrated ground truth for the visibility field and the fog nowcaster.

infrastructure.label: RTK base station
infrastructure.role: A surveyed control point broadcasting RTCM corrections over NTRIP. One base serves the whole complex.

infrastructure.label: UWB anchor
infrastructure.role: Fixed ranging reference at tip points, loading bays and the workshop gate. The places where centimetres matter and GNSS is most blocked.

rover.name: FogTwin rover prototype
rover.note: Publishes the same VehicleState schema as a production dumper, so it joins the live twin beside the simulated fleet with no special casing anywhere in the server.

tour.title: The retrofit kit
tour.body: Nothing here replaces the machine. Every part bolts onto an existing dumper inside one shift, with no OEM cooperation and no change to the driveline. NMDC will not re-fleet a hundred 100 tonne trucks, so the kit has to arrive as a bolt-on.

tour.title: Start with the physics
tour.body: The forward radar is the only sensor on this machine that still sees a dumper at 200 m in dense fog. 77 GHz is a 3.9 mm wavelength against a 10 micrometre droplet, around 390 times larger, so it passes through almost untouched. Everything optical on this truck loses to that droplet.

tour.title: Cover the geometry that kills
tour.body: Two corner units at the rear quarters. Mine accident statistics are dominated by two cases: rear-end on a ramp, and reversing over a light vehicle or a person at the tip. Both happen where the operator has no view even on a clear day.

tour.title: The sensor that replaces sight
tour.body: RTK-GNSS on the highest point of the canopy gives two to three centimetres of absolute position. The road was surveyed once, and the truck knows where it is to a few centimetres. That pair is what makes the corridor renderable with no camera involved at all.

tour.title: Decisions close on the vehicle
tour.body: The edge node fuses everything, scores collision risk, renders the HUD and caches the twin. Nothing safety-critical waits for the network. Lose comms and you lose foresight, meaning knowledge of the truck around the bend. You never lose braking.

tour.title: What the operator actually gets
tour.body: A sunlight-readable synthetic-vision display and a haptic transducer in the seat. Cab noise runs 85 to 95 dB with ear protection on, so a warning that is only audible is a warning that gets missed.

tour.title: The mine side
tour.body: Roadside units on existing lighting masts, micro-met stations spread across the elevation range, one RTK base, and UWB anchors at the tips and loading bays. All of it placed on the real Bailadila ridge against the actual haul network.

tour.title: What we actually built
tour.body: We do not have a 100 tonne dumper. We have instrumented rovers running the identical message schema, so they appear in the same twin as the simulated fleet. Every part maps to a production counterpart, and every line of software above the driver layer is unchanged.

tour.title: Power, data and cost
tour.body: One isolated supply off the machine 24 V bus, one compute hub, and a bill of materials near two lakh per vehicle. Against a single day of lost monsoon production at 37 MTPA, that is the easiest number in this project to defend.
